data.name: Jumah
data.gender_notes: Jumah is used as a male name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: In Arabic, Jumah means 'congregation' or 'assembly'. In an Islamic context, it refers to the weekly Friday prayer gathering. Jumah is a reminder of community and unity in faith. The name Jumah carries the meaning “Assembly or Congregation” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Jumah usually hope their child will grow to embody assembly or congregation and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Emblem of unity and communal prayer in Islam.
data.etymology: Jumah belongs to the Arabic linguistic tradition and is used in Islamic naming. Its recorded meaning is “Assembly or Congregation.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Jumah total 8, giving a life-path number of 8. Number 8 is linked with Saturn and with the qualities of ambition, resilience and material success.

data.cultural_impact: Jumah is an integral part of the Islamic weekly routine. The communal gathering renders a powerful sense of unity and tradition, fostering a strong bond among believers. It is a cultural practice that transcends geographical and societal boundaries, keeping the community interconnected and grounded in their faith.
data.spiritual_significance: Jumah is more than simply a weekly gathering; it is an opportunity for Muslims to reconnect spiritually and seek absolution for their sins. The communal prayer and recitation of the Quran at Jumah serves as a reminder of the oneness of Allah and the importance of maintaining a strong bond with Him. By engaging in this practice, Muslims enhance their spiritual growth, strengthen their commitment to their faith, and join collective devotion towards the Almighty.

historical_references.reference: The name Jumah is derived from the Arabic word for 'Friday'. It is believed to originate from the story of Prophet Moses (as) who was commanded by Allah to make Friday a day of congregational prayer. This practice continued and was upheld by Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) and is still observed as a weekly ritual in the Islamic community.
historical_references.context: Friday as a day of congregational prayer is mentioned in the Torah and the Bible as well. Prophet Moses (as) was commanded by Allah to make Friday a day of congregational prayer. This practice was continued and upheld by Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) and is still observed as a weekly ritual in the Islamic community.

historical_references.reference: Jumah was also the name of the Prophet Muhammad's (pbuh) companion, Abu Bakr Siddiq (ra), who was the first caliph of the Islamic State. He was known as the 'Father of the believers' and his leadership was marked by justice, fairness and wisdom. The term 'Jumah' was used as a term of respect and admiration for him.
historical_references.context: Abu Bakr Siddiq (ra) was the first caliph of the Islamic State and was known as the 'Father of the believers'. He led the Muslim community with justice, fairness and wisdom. The term 'Jumah' was used as a term of respect and admiration for him.

modern_usage.modern_context: Jumah is the Arabic term for the Friday communal Muslim prayer, which is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It is an important time for Muslims to come together to worship and connect with their community. Jumah prayers are traditionally held at mosques, but in modern times, they can also be observed online through various social media platforms. Hashtags such as #JumahPrayers and #FridayPrayers are commonly used on social media to connect Muslims around the world. Additionally, many communities hold Jumah events outside of mosques, such as interfaith gatherings and communal iftar dinners, to celebrate their Muslim identity and strengthen bonds with their neighbors.
